title: Usability Testing Guide
content: Usability testing means observing real users as they attempt realistic tasks, so the team can see where people struggle. It is the best method when the research goal is to check whether users can complete a task, such as finishing an onboarding flow. Give participants specific tasks, ask them to think aloud, and avoid helping them. Testing with around five participants per round usually reveals the most common problems. Record task success, time on task, and points where users get stuck.
inspired_by: General usability testing concepts from Nielsen Norman Group public articles

title: Accessible Forms Checklist
content: Forms must be usable by people with disabilities. Every input needs a visible label that screen readers can announce. All fields and buttons must be reachable and usable with the keyboard alone. Error messages should explain what went wrong and how to fix it, not rely on color alone. Normal text should have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background. Long workflows such as onboarding contain many forms, so they need special accessibility attention.
inspired_by: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative and WCAG 2 public guidance

title: When to Use Surveys
content: Surveys collect opinions and attitudes from many people quickly, such as satisfaction ratings or preferences. They are useful for measuring how users feel at scale. However, surveys capture what people say, not what they actually do. They are a weak choice for checking whether users can complete a task, because people often misremember or overestimate their own success. For task completion questions, observe behavior with usability testing instead.
inspired_by: General research method guidance from Nielsen Norman Group public articles
